[ir-after-all.mlir.txt](https://github.com/openxla/iree/files/14776906/ir-after-all.mlir.txt)

I'd start by fixing the npy round tripping (e.g. in https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/main/tools/test/iree-run-module-inputs.mlir). Can't fix the higher level programs if the low level tools are broken too.

Another thing we could do would be to allow ignoring some metadata when checking outputs, but that would just be a bandaid and not a robust fix.

The internals of the compiler have always been "signless integers". These are neither signed nor unsigned. Higher level tooling cares about the distinction but low level tools like iree-run-module just do what they are told.

My personal opinion is that a check tool, when confronted with a module that returns signless values and having an expected value that is sign-carrying, is well within its rights to re-interpret the result with its expecting sign semantics.

Agreed - internally we allow this signedness casting because it doesn't matter:
https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/d884c5450ff89073d56f579ba3097a290d18b61b/runtime/src/iree/modules/hal/utils/buffer_diagnostics.c#L120-L129

Ideally bindings should at most be saying e.g. "I expect this to be ui32" and then comparing what it gets back to see if it's compatible (i32, si32, ui32, etc) instead of precisely trying to match what it gets back with enum equality. Outside of tests or really sloppy runners (of which we may be one in some cases :) there's not many realistic use cases where the invoker of a function has no idea what it's getting back or how to interpret it but _also_ cares enough to fail if it doesn't exactly match.

w.r.t. numpy files: we will never be able to round-trip things correctly as numpy can't represent all of the types we can. it's also developer tooling and I don't think we really care to try to make it a source of truth for tests as it'll never be sufficient for all the tests we need to write. e.g., can't support i4, bf16, f8, etc in numpy files or any fun blocked/packed formats and we'll have to store them as opaque byte arrays and then we're back at needing the same fuzzy matching/casting as above ("do you have enough bytes/the right shape and are the bytes correct" and ignoring everything else).

A good litmus test for whether a generic test runner is depending on things it shouldn't is whether it will fail if a buffer view is returned with an `IREE_HAL_ELEMENT_TYPE_OPAQUE_*` element type and/or `IREE_HAL_ENCODING_TYPE_OPAQUE`. It's legal for the compiler/runtime to return every buffer view like that (and we will on stateless programs once we have a way to mark which state is private to the program so that we can avoid packing/unpacking state args/results between invocations).

https://github.com/nod-ai/SHARK-TestSuite/pull/146 proposed switching the comparison approach from using `iree-run-module ... --expected_output=` to using `iree-run-module ... --output=` and then loading the output into Python to use numpy comparison routines.

Looking at the C/C++ code in IREE, I think we can instead relax the metadata check here: https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/05ff73f3b4298fb63f81f5038d33bda585165694/runtime/src/iree/tooling/buffer_view_matchers.c#L267-L273 , possibly gated behind a new flag defined here: https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/05ff73f3b4298fb63f81f5038d33bda585165694/runtime/src/iree/tooling/comparison.cc#L21-L26 like
```c++
IREE_FLAG(
    bool, expected_allow_signedness_mismatches, true,
    "Allow mismatches between signless and signed types (e.g. si32 and i32)");
```

---

Another option would be switching from numpy reference output files to binary files
binary files are going to be best because of numpy not supporting all types as then you can pass in the exact types you expect per output instead of having to round-trip through numpy.

(the advantage of expected_output is that we can get reproducers that are easy to run/verify in debuggers/etc without having to use the test framework - if we dump files and then require the test runner to perform the match we'll make it harder to get standalone reproducers)

> (the advantage of expected_output is that we can get reproducers that are easy to run/verify in debuggers/etc without having to use the test framework - if we dump files and then require the test runner to perform the match we'll make it harder to get standalone reproducers)

Yep! I gave similar feedback on https://github.com/nod-ai/SHARK-TestSuite/pull/146.

> binary files are going to be best because of numpy not supporting all types as then you can pass in the exact types you expect per output instead of having to round-trip through numpy.

Sounds good. Switching test files from npy to bin would involve changing https://github.com/nod-ai/SHARK-TestSuite/blob/9464d503ddf37e658cf267254ac65a3d1f143344/iree_tests/onnx/import_tests.py#L132-L152 , possibly using code from https://github.com/nod-ai/SHARK-TestSuite/blob/9464d503ddf37e658cf267254ac65a3d1f143344/e2eshark/run.py#L255-L279. @PhaneeshB do you want to give that a try?

```
    %1 = util.call @test_add_uint8$async(%arg0, %arg1, %0, %fence) : (!hal.buffer_view, !hal.buffer_view, !hal.fence, !hal.fence) -> !hal.buffer_view
    %status = hal.fence.await until([%fence]) timeout_millis(%c-1_i32) : i32
    util.return %1 : !hal.buffer_view
  }
}

```

[ir-after-all.mlir.txt](https://github.com/openxla/iree/files/14776906/ir-after-all.mlir.txt)

I'd start by fixing the npy round tripping (e.g. in https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/main/tools/test/iree-run-module-inputs.mlir). Can't fix the higher level programs if the low level tools are broken too.

Another thing we could do would be to allow ignoring some metadata when checking outputs, but that would just be a bandaid and not a robust fix.

The internals of the compiler have always been "signless integers". These are neither signed nor unsigned. Higher level tooling cares about the distinction but low level tools like iree-run-module just do what they are told.

My personal opinion is that a check tool, when confronted with a module that returns signless values and having an expected value that is sign-carrying, is well within its rights to re-interpret the result with its expecting sign semantics.

Agreed - internally we allow this signedness casting because it doesn't matter:
https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/d884c5450ff89073d56f579ba3097a290d18b61b/runtime/src/iree/modules/hal/utils/buffer_diagnostics.c#L120-L129

Ideally bindings should at most be saying e.g. "I expect this to be ui32" and then comparing what it gets back to see if it's compatible (i32, si32, ui32, etc) instead of precisely trying to match what it gets back with enum equality. Outside of tests or really sloppy runners (of which we may be one in some cases :) there's not many realistic use cases where the invoker of a function has no idea what it's getting back or how to interpret it but _also_ cares enough to fail if it doesn't exactly match.

w.r.t. numpy files: we will never be able to round-trip things correctly as numpy can't represent all of the types we can. it's also developer tooling and I don't think we really care to try to make it a source of truth for tests as it'll never be sufficient for all the tests we need to write. e.g., can't support i4, bf16, f8, etc in numpy files or any fun blocked/packed formats and we'll have to store them as opaque byte arrays and then we're back at needing the same fuzzy matching/casting as above ("do you have enough bytes/the right shape and are the bytes correct" and ignoring everything else).

A good litmus test for whether a generic test runner is depending on things it shouldn't is whether it will fail if a buffer view is returned with an `IREE_HAL_ELEMENT_TYPE_OPAQUE_*` element type and/or `IREE_HAL_ENCODING_TYPE_OPAQUE`. It's legal for the compiler/runtime to return every buffer view like that (and we will on stateless programs once we have a way to mark which state is private to the program so that we can avoid packing/unpacking state args/results between invocations).

timeline.body:
https://github.com/nod-ai/SHARK-TestSuite/pull/146 proposed switching the comparison approach from using `iree-run-module ... --expected_output=` to using `iree-run-module ... --output=` and then loading the output into Python to use numpy comparison routines.

Looking at the C/C++ code in IREE, I think we can instead relax the metadata check here: https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/05ff73f3b4298fb63f81f5038d33bda585165694/runtime/src/iree/tooling/buffer_view_matchers.c#L267-L273 , possibly gated behind a new flag defined here: https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/05ff73f3b4298fb63f81f5038d33bda585165694/runtime/src/iree/tooling/comparison.cc#L21-L26 like
```c++
IREE_FLAG(
    bool, expected_allow_signedness_mismatches, true,
    "Allow mismatches between signless and signed types (e.g. si32 and i32)");
```

---

Another option would be switching from numpy reference output files to binary files
binary files are going to be best because of numpy not supporting all types as then you can pass in the exact types you expect per output instead of having to round-trip through numpy.

(the advantage of expected_output is that we can get reproducers that are easy to run/verify in debuggers/etc without having to use the test framework - if we dump files and then require the test runner to perform the match we'll make it harder to get standalone reproducers)

> (the advantage of expected_output is that we can get reproducers that are easy to run/verify in debuggers/etc without having to use the test framework - if we dump files and then require the test runner to perform the match we'll make it harder to get standalone reproducers)

Yep! I gave similar feedback on https://github.com/nod-ai/SHARK-TestSuite/pull/146.

> binary files are going to be best because of numpy not supporting all types as then you can pass in the exact types you expect per output instead of having to round-trip through numpy.

issue.body:
This fixes https://github.com/iree-org/iree/issues/16674 by switching from comparing against .npy files to comparing against .bin files thanks to https://github.com/nod-ai/SHARK-TestSuite/pull/212.

For example with https://github.com/nod-ai/SHARK-TestSuite/tree/main/iree_tests/onnx/node/generated/test_add_uint8:

* model.mlir:
    ```mlir
    module {
      func.func @test_add_uint8(%arg0: !torch.vtensor<[3,4,5],ui8>, %arg1: !torch.vtensor<[3,4,5],ui8>) -> !torch.vtensor<[3,4,5],ui8> attributes {torch.onnx_meta.ir_version = 7 : si64, torch.onnx_meta.opset_version = 17 : si64, torch.onnx_meta.producer_name = "backend-test", torch.onnx_meta.producer_version = ""} {
        %none = torch.constant.none
        %0 = torch.operator "onnx.Add"(%arg0, %arg1) : (!torch.vtensor<[3,4,5],ui8>, !torch.vtensor<[3,4,5],ui8>) -> !torch.vtensor<[3,4,5],ui8> 
        return %0 : !torch.vtensor<[3,4,5],ui8>
      }
    }
    ```
* `test_data_flags.txt` before:
    ```
    --input=@input_0.npy
    --input=@input_1.npy
    --expected_output=@output_0.npy
    ```

    with these errors:
    ```
    [FAILED] result[0]: metadata is 3x4x5xi8; expected that the view matches 3x4x5xui8; expected that the view is equal to contents of a view of 3x4x5xui8
    
      expected:
    
    3x4x5xui8=[[18 24 22 22 20][14 38 44 14 27][30 14 20 12 20][36 25 31 6 8]][[28 30 19 7 18][26 33 23 34 19][29 39 14 32 44][26 25 18 28 24]][[24 36 16 28 25][16 23 22 20 39][27 20 34 19 26][16 17 8 16 11]]
    
      actual:
    
    3x4x5xi8=[[18 24 22 22 20][14 38 44 14 27][30 14 20 12 20][36 25 31 6 8]][[28 30 19 7 18][26 33 23 34 19][29 39 14 32 44][26 25 18 28 24]][[24 36 16 28 25][16 23 22 20 39][27 20 34 19 26][16 17 8 16 11]]
    ```

* `test_data_flags.txt` after:
    ```
    --input=3x4x5xui8=@input_0.bin
    --input=3x4x5xui8=@input_1.bin
    --expected_output=3x4x5xi8=@output_0.bin
    ```
    (that still seems a bit mismatched? it does pass the test though)
